title: Conflicts between two sessions
intro: Pick a scenario, then watch sessions A and B run tick by tick. The model runs in your browser and never touches your data.
label: Simulated
labelNote: The result is computed by the project model, checked against real PostgreSQL in CI. It is not a run on your database, and it has no run time.

scenario.label: Scenario
scenario.deadlock_reverse_order: Deadlock from updates in reverse order

about.lost_update: Two sessions read a balance of 100, each adds its own amount and writes it back. One addition can vanish.
about.deadlock_reverse_order: Two sessions update two rows in opposite order, so each holds a lock the other needs.
about.write_skew: Two doctors each check that someone is still on call, then each goes off call. The writes hit different rows but break the same rule.
about.double_booking: Two sessions both see a free slot and both book it.
about.non_repeatable_read: One session reads the same row twice in one transaction, and another session commits in between.

tick.begin: Opens a transaction at isolation level {isolation}.
tick.waiting: Lock {resource} is held by session {holder}, so this session must wait.
tick.select: Reads data and gets {rows, plural, one {# row} other {# rows}}.
tick.update: Changes {rows, plural, one {# row} other {# rows}} and keeps their locks until commit.
tick.insert: Inserts {rows, plural, one {# row} other {# rows}}. If it is 0, the statement condition did not allow the insert.
tick.commit: Commit: this session changes are saved and its locks are released.
tick.rollback: Rollback: every change of this transaction is discarded.
tick.rollbackOfAborted: The transaction was already aborted, so this COMMIT is really a rollback and writes nothing.

error.deadlock: The two sessions wait for each other in a cycle (code 40P01). The model aborts one side so the other can continue. Real PostgreSQL may abort the other side.
error.serializeConcurrent: Another session changed and committed this row after the transaction started, so it is rejected (code 40001). The application must retry the transaction.
error.serializeDependencies: PostgreSQL found two transactions that read and write across each other in a way that cannot be put in a serial order, so it rejects the one that commits later (code 40001).
error.abortedTransaction: The transaction is in an aborted state, so every statement is ignored until rollback (code 25P02).
error.uniqueViolation: UNIQUE constraint violated: a row with the same value already exists (code 23505).

outcome.broken: Broken in this scenario at this isolation level: the final result differs from running the two sessions one after the other.
outcome.not_broken: Not broken in this scenario at this isolation level. This is the result of one two-session scenario only, not a conclusion about the whole design.
outcome.deadlock: Deadlock in this scenario: the two sessions wait for each other in a cycle and one is aborted. The model picks the aborted side, real PostgreSQL may pick the other.
outcome.serialization_failure: PostgreSQL rejects one transaction (code 40001) in this scenario at this isolation level. The application must retry that transaction.
outcome.no_criteria: No data criteria set in this scenario at this isolation level: no deadlock or serialization failure detected.

realLabelNote: Result executed and measured directly on a real database engine (MySQL 8.4 on Azure VM or PGlite in Web Worker). This is the physical reaction of the database, with no implication that the design is good or bad.

gapLock.name: The Mystery of Gap Lock Paralysis (Next-Key Lock)
gapLock.about: Session A updates a row via a non-unique index. InnoDB locks both the record and the surrounding gap (Gap Lock), causing Session B's completely independent insert to be blocked.
gapLock.learn: Lesson: In REPEATABLE READ, Next-Key Lock prevents Phantom Reads by locking gap intervals. On non-unique indexes, an UPDATE can inadvertently paralyze a large ID range, creating bottlenecks for parallel INSERTs.
gapLock.step1: Session A: Open transaction at REPEATABLE READ isolation level.
gapLock.step2: Session B: Open transaction at REPEATABLE READ isolation level.
gapLock.step3: Session A: UPDATE user_id = 10. InnoDB places Next-Key Lock on user_id=10 and Gap Lock on (10, 20).
gapLock.step4: Session B: INSERT user_id = 15. Although a fresh row, user_id=15 falls into the (10, 20) gap, immediately BLOCKING Session B!
gapLock.step5: Session A: COMMIT releases lock. Session B wakes up and completes insertion.

deadlock.name: Bank Transfer Deadlock (Error 1213)
deadlock.about: Two cross-transfer flows between Wallet 1 and Wallet 2. Each holds one wallet and waits for the other, forming an infinite wait cycle that forces MySQL engine to abort one.
deadlock.learn: Lesson: To eliminate deadlocks in banking and payments, always acquire resource locks in a globally consistent order (e.g., always lock the smaller ID first).
deadlock.step1: Session A: Begin transfer from Wallet 1 to Wallet 2.
deadlock.step2: Session B: Begin transfer from Wallet 2 to Wallet 1.
deadlock.step3: Session A: Deduct Wallet 1 (holds Exclusive Lock on Wallet 1).
deadlock.step4: Session B: Deduct Wallet 2 (holds Exclusive Lock on Wallet 2).
deadlock.step5: Session A: Credit Wallet 2 (needs Wallet 2 lock held by B -> Session A waits).
deadlock.step6: Session B: Credit Wallet 1 (attempts to lock Wallet 1 held by A -> Deadlock Cycle!). MySQL detects cycle, raises Error 1213 and aborts B.
deadlock.step7: Session A: Resumed, completes and COMMITs safely.

flashSale.name: Flash Sale Inventory Race Condition
flashSale.about: Two users simultaneously click to buy the last voucher. Both read stock = 1, resulting in negative inventory or Lost Update.
flashSale.learn: Lesson: Read-Modify-Write in default transactions is not race-free. Use Pessimistic Locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or atomic decrements (UPDATE stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock >= 1) to protect inventory.

race.step4: Session B: Read stock (also sees stock = 1 in snapshot).
race.step6: Session A: COMMIT successfully. Actual stock is now 0.
race.step7: Session B: Believing stock is still available, deducts 1 - 1 = 0 or -1! NEGATIVE INVENTORY.
race.step8: Session B: COMMIT, severe inventory loss occurred.

forUpdate.step1: Session A: Start voucher purchase with pessimistic lock.
forUpdate.step2: Session B: Start voucher purchase with pessimistic lock.
forUpdate.step3: Session A: SELECT stock ... FOR UPDATE (reads 1 and locks record exclusively).
forUpdate.step4: Session B: SELECT stock ... FOR UPDATE -> BLOCKED and queues orderly behind A!
forUpdate.step5: Session A: Deduct stock and complete payment.
forUpdate.step6: Session A: COMMIT releases lock. Session B wakes up and reads latest stock = 0!
forUpdate.step7: Session B: Sees stock = 0, notices out-of-stock and performs safe ROLLBACK.

dirtyRead.name: Dirty Read at READ UNCOMMITTED
dirtyRead.about: Session B lowers isolation to READ UNCOMMITTED and reads Session A's uncommitted interim balance. When Session A rolls back, Session B holds dirty/phantom data.
dirtyRead.learn: Lesson: PostgreSQL doesn't suffer Dirty Reads because its engine treats READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED. MySQL allows it, and in financial apps, Dirty Reads can cause massive losses if decisions rely on uncommitted data.
dirtyRead.step1: Session A: Open transaction at READ COMMITTED.
dirtyRead.step2: Session B: Open transaction at READ UNCOMMITTED.
dirtyRead.step3: Session A: Update balance to 500 without COMMIT.
dirtyRead.step4: Session B: Reads balance as 500 even though A never committed! DIRTY READ.
dirtyRead.step5: Session A: Encounters error and ROLLBACKs all changes.
dirtyRead.step6: Session B: Reads again and sees balance restored to original 100. The 500 was a ghost!
